findings.title: Completing one work order returned a still-faulty device to clinical service, across any tenant, any number of times
findings.description:
BiomedicalService.complete_work_order carried three defects on a LIVE, migration-backed table (biomed_work_orders) reachable at POST /biomedical/work-orders/{wo_id}/complete.

(1) The lookup was filter_by(id=wo_id) with no tenant predicate, and the service had no tenant context at all to scope it with. A caller acting for lab A completed lab B's work order and flipped lab B's device to available. The router requires system:admin, but admin is a lab-scoped role here — only master_admin and ministry_admin are cross-tenant — so this was a genuine cross-tenant mutation, not an intended override.

(2) Closing ANY work order set device.status = AVAILABLE unconditionally. A class III ventilator held out_of_service with two open work orders became available when only the first was completed; the second fault was never touched. Returning a device to clinical service is a safety decision, and closing one ticket says nothing about the faults the other tickets were raised for.

(3) No row lock and no terminal-state guard: two concurrent transactions both committed the same terminal transition, the later write silently replaced the earlier one's cost and action record, and `version` never moved off 1 although the model carries the optimistic-lock column.

findings.title: 28 mutating service methods select a row by id with no tenant predicate anywhere in the method
findings.description:
The defect fixed in NR-016 is an instance of a pattern, not a one-off. An AST pass over backend/app found 28 mutating methods (they set .status, commit, or delete) whose row lookup is filter_by(id=...) and which contain no lab_id or tenant reference anywhere in the method body.

By domain: blood_bank 5, critical_care 4, lifecycle_platform 4, national/notification_platform 4, biomedical 3, command_center 2, document_intelligence 2, ems 2, pilot_platform 1, public_health 1.

A second pass split them by whether the method name is called from any api/routes module: 24 apparently route-reachable, 4 not.

CAVEAT, stated because it changes what this number means. The reachability test matches on method NAME, so generic names over-count: the four notification_platform save()/delete() hits and the two document_intelligence delete()/unregister() hits are very likely matching an unrelated class. Treat 24 as an upper bound, not a count of confirmed live holes. Only NR-016 was individually traced end to end and reproduced.

THE 4 NOT ROUTE-REACHABLE ARE INFORMATIVE. blood_bank start_transfusion() and complete_transfusion() are tenant-blind but SUPERSEDED: the routes call start_transfusion_safely() and complete_transfusion_safely(transfusion_id, lab_id, body), which do take the tenant. So the earlier blood-bank hardening left the unscoped originals in place rather than removing them. They are dead weight that reads like a live hole and would become one if anything called them again.

TRACED 2026-09-25, and the heuristic's over-count is now demonstrated twice:
  critical_care.discharge_patient() — SAFE / DEAD-SUPERSEDED. The route calls discharge_patient_safely(admission_id, body, lab_id), which has the lab filter, .with_for_update(), is_deleted, a terminal-state guard over {discharged, transferred, deceased}, required-field validation, version += 1 and a bed lock with an ownership check — wrapped by ClinicalCommandGuard with If-Match and an idempotency key. findings.title: HospitalService._get_entity compiled to WHERE false, so ten hospital routes answered 404 for records that exist
findings.description: The helper filtered with Python's 'not' instead of SQLAlchemy's '~': db.query(model).filter(model.id == entity_id, model.lab_id == lab_id, not model.is_deleted). model.is_deleted is an InstrumentedAttribute with no __bool__ override, so bool(...) is default object truthiness (True) and 'not model.is_deleted' is the literal False. SQLAlchemy folds a AND b AND false to false, so the compiled statement was 'WHERE false' — the id and tenant predicates did not fail to match, they were eliminated. The helper never returned a row and always raised NotFoundError. All ten route call sites in app/routes/hospital.py were affected, including assign_bed, discharge_bed, transfer_bed, update_department, and complete_surgical_safety_checklist.

findings.description: An InstrumentedAttribute does not override __bool__, so 'not Model.attr' is the literal False. SQLAlchemy accepts it into the WHERE clause and folds the conjunction (a AND b AND false is false), compiling to 'WHERE false' and ELIMINATING every other predicate in the same call, lab_id included. An AST sweep found 28 such predicates: 20 in app/lims/routes.py (Department, Instrument, InstrumentModel, Manufacturer, Specimen, Order, Panel, Result, QCProgram, Reagent, Consumable, Lot, Supplier, Storage, ReferenceRangeDef, DeltaCheckRule, AutoValidationRule, LabReport), 3 in app/pharmacy/inventory.py and services.py (batch selection excluded every batch rather than only quarantined ones), 1 in app/pharmacy/routes.py (_get_or_404 could never find a row), 3 in app/radiology/pacs.py (an image share could not be resolved or revoked) and 1 in app/routes/admin.py (the lab-approval queue was permanently empty, so no registered lab could be activated).

findings.title: Four administrative modules carried no authorization on any route, and the API-spec surface bypassed the production docs guard
findings.description: app/identity/lifecycle/routes.py (42 routes: enterprise registration, licensing, inspection, risk assessment), app/lifecycle_platform/api/routes.py (components, releases, compatibility, upgrade paths, deprecations), app/pilot_platform/api/routes.py (15 routes: national pilot deployment and readiness gates) and app/certification/routes.py (9 routes: release certification and gates) had zero guards between them. Separately, DocsAuthMiddleware protected {/docs, /redoc, /openapi.json} as an exact-match set, while app/contracts/routes.py regenerates the same surface — OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, per-module JSON Schema and the FHIR R4 profiles — under its own prefix, so the specification the platform deliberately protects in production was served unauthenticated at /contracts/openapi.json.

findings.root_cause: Two modules independently claimed the same prefix.
findings.evidence: Both router definitions read directly; found while guarding them, when a router-level guard applied to one module did not protect /lifecycle/components because that path belongs to the other.
findings.operational_impact: A path served by whichever router registered first. No collision was observed between the specific paths exercised, but the namespace is ambiguous by construction.
findings.recommended_fix: Give one of them a distinct prefix. Which module keeps /lifecycle is an ownership decision, and renaming a served prefix is an API contract change.
findings.minimal_safe_fix: NOT APPLIED. Both routers are now guarded, so the security consequence is closed; the naming remains.
findings.verification_method: Once a prefix is chosen: assert no two routers share a prefix.
findings.acceptance_criteria: Each router prefix is claimed by exactly one module.
findings.regression_risk: Renaming a prefix breaks any client using it.
findings.evidence_strength: STRONG on the collision (both definitions read); no shadowing incident observed.
findings.status: OPEN — RECORDED, not resolved. Deciding which module owns the prefix is an ownership question.
findings.title: Two routers share the /lifecycle prefix
findings.description: app/identity/lifecycle/routes.py and app/lifecycle_platform/api/routes.py both register with prefix="/lifecycle". They serve different domains — identity lifecycle (enterprise registration, licensing) versus platform lifecycle (components, releases, deprecations) — under one namespace, so paths from the two can shadow each other depending on registration order.
